title: Ad Extirpanda: Pope Innocent IV Authorizes Torture in Heresy Trials
description: Pope Innocent IV's bull Ad Extirpanda (1252) authorized the use of torture by inquisitors against heretics — a critical procedural development that enabled the systematic extraction of confessions throughout heresy and later witchcraft proceedings. The bull permitted torture to the point of serious mutilation but not death, and required confessions obtained under torture to be ratified freely the following day — a requirement frequently violated in practice. This papal authorization legitimized torture as an inquisitorial tool within a framework that presumed guilt and valued confession above all other evidence. The procedural framework established by Ad Extirpanda and subsequent amplifications made it possible to extract elaborate confessions about sabbaths, diabolical pacts, and names of accomplices.
historiographical_note: Carlo Ginzburg's microhistorical methodology foregrounds the torture context of all witch confessions — his analysis of the benandanti in Night Battles shows how interrogators' questions shaped and distorted original folk beliefs. The authorization of torture in 1252 is therefore not merely a procedural detail but a fundamental shaping force in what witchcraft confessions claimed.
source_method: Papal registers; Corpus Iuris Canonici; secondary scholarship on inquisitorial procedure
